messages.subject: n_eff query
parts:
Regarding n_eff - what sort of size should it be as a rule of thumb, I've been aiming for about 1,000 as a guide, and some of my data models do this easily for N=1000 and chains=4 - but others don't... not by a long shot!

When doing comparative marginal density plots of different sets of data on the same model, I assume that it would be appropriate to re-run the model with a bigger N until I get at least the same order of magnitude for n_eff?

Has anybody done this in R?

Thanks in advance,

Kind regards,

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] n_eff query
parts:
n_eff is an indication of your Monte Carlo error, i.e. the error introduced from approximating your expectations with Monte Carlo averages. 
In particular, if the marginal distribution for one of your parameters has mean mu and standard deviation sigma then the Monte Carlo average
will converge to N( <x> | mu, sigma / sqrt(n_eff) ).

How large n_eff should be then depends on your application.  In inference tasks typical to our applications, the mean only needs to be known
with precision relative to the standard deviation and n_eff = 100 is a good rule of thumb.  If the absolute precision is important, however,
then n_eff might have to be taken as much larger in order to achieve the desired threshold.

If you're running the same model and just varying the data you might be running into problems with adaptation getting stuck so watch out
for the tuning parameters.  In any case, for an honest comparison by eye you should indeed re-run until all models have the same n_eff.
Any numerical comparisons can always be corrected by weighted the two samples by their respective n_eff.
